title: Mata Gujri
hookLine: wife of the ninth Guru, mother of the tenth, grandmother of the Sahibzade, steady to the end

cards: Near the town of Sirhind, in Punjab, there's a gurdwara called Fatehgarh Sahib, and close by stands a place Sikhs call the Thanda Burj, the cold tower. Some visitors stand there a long time, in no hurry.
Others bring their children and grandchildren and tell them a story there, the same story a grandmother once told there to her small grandsons, on cold nights.

teach.b: Mata Gujri's life runs through three generations of the Guru's house. She was the wife of Guru Tegh Bahadur, with him in the quiet years at Bakala.

She was the mother of Guru Gobind Singh, and grandmother to the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. She saw her husband leave for Delhi, where, Sikhs remember, he gave his life rather than let others be forced from their faith.
She raised her son to lead. Then came the hardest winter.

Tradition says that when the Guru's family left Anandpur under attack, they were scattered at a flooded river crossing. Mata Gujri ended up alone with her youngest grandsons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh.

A former servant of the household, Gangu, took them in, and then, tradition says, betrayed them to the authorities. They were taken to Sirhind and held in the cold tower. Tradition remembers what she did there.
She didn't panic, and she didn't tell the boys to save themselves at any cost. She told them about their grandfather, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the Gurus before him.
She kept them steady. Brought before the governor, the boys refused to give up their faith, and they were put to death. Tradition says Mata Gujri died in the tower soon after.
Sikhs also remember who spoke up.
Tradition says the Nawab of Malerkotla, a Muslim noble, protested that children should not be punished this way, and a local man, Todar Mal, gave what he had so they could be cremated with honor.
Steady to the end, here, isn't the absence of grief. It's a grandmother who stayed herself, and kept her grandsons steady, until the very end.

how: Sikhs remember Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade each winter, especially at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind, with prayer, kirtan and the retelling of their story.

games.q: you're Mata Gujri in the cold tower with your grandsons, the night before they face the governor. what do you do?
o: tell them to say whatever will save them.
tell them about their grandfather and the Gurus before him, and keep them steady.
keep silent so as not to frighten them.
games.why: tradition says she told them the stories of their family and kept them steady; the boys held to their faith.

practice: Bring to mind a grandmother: your own, someone else's, or an older woman who steadied you when you were young.

See her hands and one thing she used to say; if she's living, think of one way to honor her this week, and if she's gone, simply thank her in your mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
